Frames

Schema definition and guidance.

Race Report

Race results and incidents over Aintree’s National fences

Coverage of specific race outcomes and in-race happenings at Aintree over the Grand National fences (including the Grand National, Topham, Sefton, Grand Sefton), focusing on finish order, fallers, unseats, and race dynamics.

Keywords: Grand National, Aintree, National fences, Topham Handicap Chase, Grand Sefton, Becher's Brook, finish, winner, runner-up, fell, unseated, pulled up, crossed the line, failed to finish, dramatic race

Examples: "Peter Bowen extended his remarkable record in the Topham Handicap Chase over the Grand National fences here on Friday, as Mac Tottie, at 8-1, crossed the line in front after a dramatic race in which 11 of the 29 runners failed to finish."; "Three horses departed at the ninth fence, as Foxy Jacks fell and rolled to his left, bringing down Colorado Doc and Discordantly."

Safety & Welfare

Equine and rider safety, welfare outcomes, and risk context at Aintree

Focus on health outcomes, injuries or lack thereof, medical response, risk/safety protocols, and welfare status of horses and riders in the Grand National/Aintree context.

Keywords: safety, risk, welfare, injured, unhurt, fatality, fatal fall, euthanised, put down, veterinary, vet, ambulance, medical team, stewards' inquiry, screens, equine welfare

Examples: "All horses and jockeys were later reported to be unhurt."; "Two fallers at Becher's were reported uninjured after the Grand National."

Betting & Odds

Betting markets, tips, prices, and wagering on the Grand National

Coverage of odds, tips, staking advice, favourites, and wagering anecdotes related to the Grand National/Aintree meeting.

Keywords: odds, price, SP, ante-post, market, favourite, outsider, each-way, nap, tip, punt, bet, flutter, selection, accumulator, longshot

Examples: "I had a little flutter on the Grand National"; "Quick Guide Greg Wood's Saturday tips Show Aintree ... 5.15 Longhouse Poet (nap)"

Celebs & Style

Celebrities, attendees, and fashion at Aintree

Lifestyle coverage of famous attendees, crowd scenes, fashion and outfits (e.g., Ladies Day) around the Grand National meeting.

Keywords: celebrity, famous faces, TV stars, red carpet, fashion, outfits, Ladies Day, style, glamour, crowd, attendees, photos, gallery

Examples: "The Grand National is now well into its second day, and among the thousands of people to visit Aintree Racecourse were some famous faces."; "Many people arrived in their finest outfits, all geared up for a great day out at the races."

Records & Connections

Trainer/jockey achievements, records, and stable narratives

Pieces centered on trainers, jockeys, and stables achieving milestones, setting/equalling records, or discussing preparation and roles, often with quotes from connections.

Keywords: record, milestone, fifth winner, equalling, trainer said, jockey said, stable, connections, preparation, schooling, No 1 rider, family operation, brilliant, get one ready

Examples: "Mac Tottie was Bowen’s fifth Topham winner, equalling Nicky Henderson’s record, and added to the same horse’s success over the National fences in the Grand Sefton Chase in November."; "I’m not being biased but Dad is brilliant," Sean Bowen said. "When he wants to get one ready, he gets one ready."

National Aims

Entries, targets, and future plans aimed at the Grand National

Forward-looking coverage about entries, weights, suitability, and plans to run in the Grand National, including speculation that a horse is being aimed at or qualifies as a National type.

Keywords: entry, entries, declared, weights, handicap, aimed at, targeting, National horse, get the trip, plans to run, go next year, line up, field

Examples: "If he gets the trip, he might be a National horse, maybe we’ll have a go next year."; "Connections confirmed he will be aimed at the Grand National."

GN Metaphor

Grand National used as comparison or cultural reference

Mentions of the Grand National as an analogy, benchmark, or attendance comparison in unrelated contexts, not actual coverage of the Aintree event.

Keywords: like the Grand National, no different to the Grand National, more than the Grand National, surpassing the Grand National, Grand National crowds, metaphor, analogy, comparison

Examples: "no different to the grand national."; "The spectacle attracted crowds of many thousands, surpassing those at both the Derby and the Grand National that year."

🔗📁Haydock’s Grand National Trial (15:15) is the feature handicap this weekend and with Storms Ciara and Dennis doing their worst the going will be heavy. Haydock’s heavy ground is notoriously heavy, and it could really pay to side with a lightly weighted runner. One that catches the eye is the 11-year-old Smooth Stepper who gets in here off 10-0 (9-11 in the long handicap) but even the 3lb extra he has to carry means he’s still running off a handicap mark of 136, which is below his highest and last winning mark of 138. That victory also came on heavy ground and over three mile two furlongs and given he carries such a low weight I think he can run a massive race at a huge price.

🔗📁Jan is a barmaid at the working men’s club of a depressed Welsh pit village. She has a dream: to rear a racehorse and break into the sport of kings. It’s an unlikely ambition. A horse with prospects can cost hundreds of thousands of pounds and yet more on top to train, though only one percent of tyro steeds ever win a race. Still, Jan cajoles a few of her regulars and other village characters into joining her project. Some of them are unemployed, but each promises to put up £10 a week for purchase, stud fees, training, race entry payments and jockey charges.

🔗📁He finished 11th in the Pertemps Final at the Cheltenham Festival in his prep race earlier this month. He finished third in the same race prior to his National victory, but Newland was happy with that effort. He said: “His form is okay. It has been a different campaign to last year because last year we had to get into the race and we were racing a lot more. We had to win a race to qualify – which we did at Exeter. But this year we knew we would be in the race, so it was all about getting back in one piece. So we have deliberately gone slowly, slowly. Possibly too slowly, but I have been happy with his two runs. Two good runs over hurdles. Not many 12-year-old National winners could be running in Pertemps Finals and giving weight to horses who he is twice the age of. I think he has run well enough.”

🔗📁Boy, 13, dies after pony racing accident Jack de Bromhead, the 13-year-old son of dual Gold Cup-winning trainer Henry de Bromhead, sustained fatal injuries Henry de Bromhead's son Jack pictured with his mother Heather (Image: Harry Murphy/Sportsfile via Getty Images) The racing community was in mourning on Sunday following the death of Jack de Bromhead, the 13-year-old son of dual Gold Cup-winning trainer Henry de Bromhead, in a pony racing accident on Saturday. The teenager sustained fatal injuries in an incident during the fifth race on the first day of the Glenbeigh Festival in County Kerry, Ireland. Gardai and emergency services were called to the scene at Rossbeigh beach at approximately 5.20pm, where the young rider received treatment but was later pronounced dead. The event was immediately cancelled.

🔗📁A Virtual Grand National - won by Potters Corner - captured the attention of the public but the British Horseracing Authority are keen to return 'at the earliest point conditions allow'. The big thing for every sport is returning and being able to stage events without putting too much strain on health services at such a precarious time. Any return would likely see a reduction in the number of competitors per race and no spectators for events, including Royal Ascot, which has been slated for June 16. Having held Cheltenham Festival with thousands of spectators each day - a decision later criticised - as other sports went into lockdown, racing may well look to be the first to test the waters in getting back underway.

🔗📁Townend was aboard the other co-favourite. Not that you would have realised that in the early stages. Riding the horse from the Willie Mullins stable, owned by the serial Irish winner JP McManus, Townend bided his time. For much of the first loop of Aintree’s course, the French horse Glengouly led the way. I Am Maximus was tucked in on the inside, keeping his pace in reserve. At the Chair on the first lap he stumbled. “I thought he’d let Paul out over his ears,” said Mullins. “Paul told me afterwards he was only doing enough to get over the fences, and he clipped a couple of others too. It’s probably the way to do Aintree rather than big extravagant jumps that sap energy. But I admit I was worried.”

🔗📁The changes that were introduced included the adapting and rebuilding of fences, facilities and stables, while new approaches and bypass areas to the fences have been added to improve safety for the horses. However, following the death of Solwara One - trained by Neil Mulholland - a spokesperson for the RSPCA said: "We are deeply saddened and concerned after the death of Solwara One at the Aintree Grand National Meeting. The death of any horse is always one too many so it is crucial that steps are taken to reduce the risk of such tragedies occurring." ‌ Eclair Surf Animal Aid’s Horse Racing Campaigner, Jade Emery, called for the event to be banned completely. She said: "If a horse’s life is worthless to the racing industry, as we have seen every year at the Grand National meeting, then the industry itself is devoid of morals. It’s time to challenge the acceptance of this race meeting, and the associated deaths, and see it banned from taking place."

🔗📁Popular Horse Racing Betting Types This next section will discuss some of the most popular betting options for fans of horse racing betting. Make sure to read on to learn more. Race Winner A race-winner bet is rather self-explanatory in that it is simply when a player places a bet on which horse they believe will win a certain race. Therefore in order for a player to be paid out as a winner, they must back the horse that goes on to win the race. Each-Way An each-way bet is a bet where half of the total stakes are for the selection to win, and the other half is for the selection to be placed. If this selection wins, the win portion is then calculated in the normal way. The placed portion, however, is settled at a fraction of the win odds.

🔗📁Bet Through The Card This is not a particularly common promotion. However, it is still exceptionally rewarding for players. Bet through the card essentially means that a bookmaker may have a promo that states, for example, “Bet £10 on the first race at Cheltenham on a selected day and get a £5 free bet on the next six races of the day.” Therefore, players receive an incentive to bet through the race card for that day. All of the best horse racing betting sites will potentially offer this for major events. Price Promise A price promise is, again, rather self-explanatory in the fact that it is when a bookmaker promises to offer customers the best odds in the industry. Therefore, if you place a bet on a horse to win, and it comes first, the bookmaker will offer you the best (or joint best) odds in the industry. For example, if the site you are betting on has the horse you wish to bet on at 4/1 to win, but another site has the same horse to win the same race at 6/1, the site you are on will match or better those odds.

🔗📁News | UK Police arrested 118 people at Aintree Racecourse as large numbers of protesters attempted to gain entry to the track – delaying the start of the flagship Grand National. Scores of activists climbed fences at Aintree, with at least two fixing themselves to a jump using glue and lock-on devices, animal rights group Animal Rising said. The protesters breached security fences as National runners were in the parade ring, causing a delay of 12 minutes, although racegoers helped police and event organisers to stop some from reaching the track. When the race started, a horse was destroyed after falling at the first fence – the second to die at Aintree on Saturday and the third at the three-day festival – prompting campaigners to call for jump racing to be banned.

🔗📁This was a race of reduced numbers, foreshortened at the start to prevent horses arriving at the first fence overexcited. The restricted field of 34 was further reduced to 32 by two non-runners, Chambard and Run Wild Fred, to leave the smallest number of entries for a quarter of a century. And the safety measures seemed to work: this was the first National since 2018 not to precipitate an equine fatality. Indeed there was only one faller: Corach Rambler, last year’s winner and this year’s co-favourite, which hit the turf while loose as it negotiated the second fence, having unseated 2023’s winning jockey Davy Russell at the first.

🔗📁Given his reputation as one of the world's great sportsmen, a man who has dominated his profession for 18 years, the fair market rate for his services should probably be more than double the average. It would, of course, mean that some who use him now might look for a cheaper option – fewer rides, therefore, and fewer winners but a higher income in the end. A few years ago Britain's jockeys collectively chewed over the question of whether the time had come to end the culture of the flat fee, letting each rider charge as he or she pleased. "It never got past first base," recalls Mick Fitzgerald, who, as a high-profile jump jockey at the time, would have had something to gain from a free market but spoke against it anyway. "The general feeling was that a lot of lads do the same job, they take the same risks and they deserve to be rewarded accordingly," he said on Sunday.

🔗📁Fletcher also struck gold with Red Alligator, but it was his wins on Ginger McCain's Red Rum that propelled the jockey into the spotlight RACING MOURNS Grand National winner Brian Fletcher, who rode Red Rum to win the race twice has died, aged 69 BRIAN FLETCHER, who rode three winners of the Grand National including two on Red Rum, has died, aged 69. Fletcher first came to prominence at Aintree when he steered Red Alligator to third place in the famous renewal won by Foinavon in 1967, when just a 19-year-old. He made no mistake the following year on the Denys Smith-trained Red Alligator and went on to become part of Aintree folklore for his wins on Ginger McCain’s Red Rum.

🔗📁Aintree has thrown a ring of steel around the famous Grand National course at the start of the three-day racing festival. In the wake of the terror attacks in Paris and Brussels , race-goers faced added security measures as they arrived at the course. All cars were checked inside and out, with drivers and passengers asked to leave their vehicles as the sweeps were completed. Engine compartments and boots were all thoroughly inspected. And security guards used military-style under-car mirrors to check for explosive devices. Metal detectors, body and bag searches were also in use. Punters arriving for Friday’s packed out Ladies Day on Merseyside have been warned to arrive early to avoid long queues at the entrances. Police say there have not been any direct threats to the race meeting. Read more: Brussels ISIS bomber 'worked as cleaner in European Parliament' But they want to ensure race-goers feel safe and secure throughout the event. One security worker said: “It’s ramped up from what we did before, as a lot of things have happened recently haven’t they?”

🔗📁But he would not be so close to 4,000 were it not for an oddity about the way jockeys conduct their business: they all cost the same. If your horse runs tomorrow and you hire McCoy, his fee will be £157.72. Should you choose instead a jockey who has not won all year, his fee will also be £157.72 and, in the event of success, you would have to pay them an identical share of the prize money. The same is true of Flat jockeys, though their fee is around £40 less. Baffling though it may appear, it costs no more to leg-up Frankie Dettori than someone who has not booted home all seven winners on a valuable card at Ascot.

🔗📁Because Waley-Cohen is an amatuer, he won't receive any prize money for winning the world-famous race. The 39-year-old has a day job running a successful dentistry business. Article continues below Father Robert, who watched his son win the Grand National on a horse he owns in his last race, told ITV: "It's a dream come true. Just fabulous. It's a team and thank God it has really worked. He has so much dedication and puts in so much hard work." The total prize fund for the Grand National in 2022 was £1,000,000, with £531,600 going to the winning owner. Some jockeys have personal arrangements with owners and they may receive a riders' retainers fee for riding all that owner's horses. Winning jockeys received a percentage of the prize money, typically around 8 per cent for a winning ride or 4 per cent for a placed finish according to grandnational.org.

🔗📁To kick-start the process, Jan empties her building society account without telling her husband and picks up a dud-looking mare for £350. She gets it sired by a clapped-out stallion for another £3,500 (plus VAT). The syndicate raise the resulting foal on a slagheap allotment and name him Dream Alliance after themselves. A couple of years later they’ve saved enough money to pay back Jan and hire a top trainer. Dream seems slow and unpromising, but on his debut run at Newbury he manages to come fourth. On his next outing, at Cheltenham, he takes second place. In his fourth race, at Chepstow, he stuns the racing world by outstripping fancied thoroughbreds to come first. Later, setbacks occur. Then disaster strikes. Yet in an apparently impossible comeback, Dream wins the Welsh Grand National, to be acclaimed by the tabloids as the “Slumnag Millionaire”. After another dramatic and emotional twist, he’s forced into honourable retirement, but his earnings leave syndicate members boasting a profit.

🔗📁“He’s only a small, little horse but he has such heart,” Gavin Cromwell said of Raz De Maree, who made him the second trainer to win a Welsh Grand National from Ireland. A farrier by trade, Cromwell has shod Gold Cup and Grand National winners for other people but has now won a major race of his own after a 13-year training career. It was a desire to avoid breaking Raz De Maree’s enormous heart that prompted Cromwell to book James Bowen, believed to be the youngest winning rider in this race’s rich history. With an established jockey, the horse would have had to shoulder more than 11 stone, the kind of burden under which he has struggled in the past. Bowen’s 5lb claim, granted by the rules to compensate for his inexperience, was reckoned by the trainer to be gold dust for a race run on such a stamina-sapping surface.

🔗📁Police arrested 118 people at Aintree Racecourse as large numbers of protesters attempted to gain entry to the track – delaying the start of the flagship Grand National. Scores of activists climbed fences at Aintree, with at least two fixing themselves to a jump using glue and lock-on devices, animal rights group Animal Rising said. The protesters breached security fences as National runners were in the parade ring, causing a delay of 12 minutes, although racegoers helped police and event organisers to stop some from reaching the track. A horse was destroyed after falling at the first fence – the second to die at Aintree on Saturday and the third at the three-day festival – prompting campaigners to call for jump racing to be banned.

🔗📁Trixie A Trixie is when a player places a multiple bet consisting of four bets involving three selections in different events. This bet includes three doubles and one treble. But unlike an accumulator, a minimum of two selections must win in order for a player to be paid out as a winner. Yankee Similar to a Trizie, a Yankee is when a player places a multiple bet consisting of 11 bets. This includes six doubles, four trebles and one four-fold. This is placed on four selections in different events. Again, at least two selections must be successful in order for the player to be paid out as a winner.

The Long Mile had to be put down after suffering a fatal injury during the 2021 Grand National, with Up For Review also losing his life at the Aintree racecourse two years earlier. Changes to the course were introduced in 2012 and there were no fatalities between 2013 and 2018, but that has now increased to five in the last three runnings of the festival (2020 was cancelled due to Covid-19).

🔗📁Ranking a 1-2-3 where Walsh, McCoy and Geraghty are concerned is pointless, as all three riders contributed so much to so many great moments for National Hunt racing, and at Cheltenham in particular, while the meeting continued to grow in scale and significance to become one of the country’s biggest sporting events. Walsh had more winners at the Festival, retiring last April with 59, while McCoy racked up 20 straight championships in Britain and more than 4,000 winners in all. But McCoy’s career total of 31 Festival winners is some way adrift of Geraghty’s 43, and his clear second place in the all-time list is unlikely to be challenged for many years to come.

🔗📁Saturday’s race was run at a good pace from the off on ground that was officially soft after overnight rain. Cue Card, last year’s winner, set out to make the running but was not allowed an easy lead by his rivals and his jumping showed the pressure as he made several mistakes down the back. He faded quickly in the straight as Noel Fehily, on Silviniaco Conti, struck for home, and while Menorah, from the in-form yard of Philip Hobbs, set off in pursuit, he never seemed likely to close the gap completely as Silviniaco Conti stayed on grimly for a two-length success. Dynaste, who finished second 12 months ago, was another eight lengths back in third.

🔗📁Aintree Racecourse is hosting a 'Summer Nights - Sounds of the 80s' music and racing fixture on Friday, May 15 featuring several big names act from the decade. An evening of Jump racing will precede performances from three of the biggest and best names of music in the 1980s, with another act to be announced for the live open air concert in the Red Rum Garden. Heading the showcase of 80s talent will be famous pop duo, Go West. They will be performing their hit singles Call Me, We Close Our Eyes and King of Wishful Thinking. Joining Go West will be Liverpool favourites, The Christians who will perform hits such as Ideal World, Words and Harvest for the World. There will also be an appearance by Eurovision Song Contest runner-up, Sonia who will perform a repertoire including her UK no.1 single, You'll Never Stop Me Loving You.

🔗📁Horse Racing Live Streaming The ability to live stream the top horse races in the world is something that all of the top horse racing betting sites should strive to deliver. Therefore, it is crucial that all of the best horse racing betting sites provide their customers with ample live-streaming services. Some sites may have some requirements that must be met in order to be able to live stream certain horse racing events. These requirements may state that customers must have an active bet on that specific race in order to be able to watch. Others may require a pre-paid and funded account in order to be eligible to live stream certain races.

🔗📁There were times, such as the spring of 2003 when a 23-year-old Geraghty won the first of two awards for the top rider at Cheltenham, when he seemed to have no equals in producing a flawless ride when it mattered most. Geraghty’s five winners that year – doubles on Tuesday and Thursday, with Moscow Flyer’s first Champion Chase on the middle day - equalled the record for a three-day Festival. Just over three weeks later, he landed the Grand National on Monty’s Pass. Quick Guide Pinatubo bounces back with Prix Jean Prat win Show Pinatubo got back on the winning trail with a stylish victory in the Qatar Prix Jean Prat at Deauville. The 1-2 favourite, dropped to seven furlongs for this Group One race after two recent defeats, made his backers sweat before pulling away under William Buick. Charlie Appleby's stable star was crowned last season's champion two-year-old after an unbeaten six-race campaign, but came third in the 2,000 Guineas and lost to Palace Pier in the St James's Palace Stakes at Ascot. Pinatubo got back to form here despite getting stuck in a pocket for the first half of the race as he tracked fellow British raider Molatham.

🔗📁That day he could be called the winner a long way from home. It looked as though his jockey, Barry Geraghty, could have put him anywhere in the packed field that he wished and Geraghty was in the enviable position of being able to wait for a stride or two after hitting the front before asking for a final effort. If the horse tackles this track in a similar mood, he will have a better chance than most of picking his way through any trouble that happens in front of him. The Druids Nephew is only eight years old, younger than most Grand National winners, but this is his third season over fences and he has had plenty of experience. Importantly he has shown enormous improvement since joining the very promising young trainer Neil Mulholland about a year ago. Mulholland says the horse has been trained through the winter with the twin targets of Cheltenham and Aintree in mind.

🔗📁The ease of Might Bite’s success, which was sealed with a flourish as he flew the last fence, was all the more impressive in view of his hard race behind Native River on heavy ground at Cheltenham last month. He will now head to summer quarters as the ante‑post favourite for both the King George VI Chase and Gold Cup next season, while Henderson may also consider a run in the Betfair Chase in November to set up a possible tilt at a £1m bonus on offer for victory in all three races. “He’s been fresh and well since Cheltenham and you’d have thought he’d have been the one who wouldn’t be as he had such a gruelling race at the Festival,” Henderson said. “He’s not a fragile horse in any sense but you always have to be wary of his head, so it was quite brave coming here and I had my doubts. His jumping was an exhibition round. The plan will be the same next year and I’d love to have another crack at the Gold Cup on good ground.”

🔗📁The Grand National Festival got underway on Thursday and many of those in attendance were left scratching their eyes after seeing the price of alcohol at Aintree. It was an action-packed first day with Constitution Hill falling for the second time in succession as Lossiemouth landed the William Hill Aintree Hurdle. Over 20,000 people made their way to the racecourse, which is situated on the outskirts of Liverpool. It was a glorious Ladies Day in terms of weather and naturally most were keen to get their hands on a drink following their arrival. However, they may have decided to limit their intake after seeing the prices of alcohol at the event.

🔗📁Indeed, it said plenty that he was sent off an 11-4 poke against horses with far inferior ability in what can only be described as a resurrection mission. But as soon as the tape went up, it was clear he was back. He travelled with the zest that had been absent for so long, jumped like a dream under Paddy Brennan and careered away for an emphatic victory. It began a resurgence that saw him land another Betfair Chase and a King George, before a third-last flight tumble in the Cheltenham Gold Cup left the racing world thinking what might have been.

🔗📁‌ Chris Proudman, Veterinary Advisor to Aintree Racecourse, told The Mirror : “We were sad to learn that Eclair Surf had to be put to sleep this morning. 🔗📁Dr Richard Newland is hopeful Pineau De Re is in the good enough form as he heads back to Aintree to defend his Crabbie’s Grand National crown. Pineau De Re is a 25-1 chance with several firms including Ladbrokes, William Hill, BetVictor and Paddy Power to become the first horse since Red Rum in 1973-74 to win back-to-back renewals of the Grand National at Aintree two weeks on Saturday. Newland and Pineau De Re’s owner, Glaswegian John Provan, were both back at Aintree for the Northern Media Lunch when the latest entries were unveiled yesterday. And they are hopeful of enjoying more success.

🔗📁It's a legal requirement that t's and c's are in place for a promotion. However, it's always worth scrolling through the key elements to understand how an offer works. Sometimes the biggest free bets aren't always the most generous. That's because you may be required to bet any winnings a number of times before a withdrawal can be made. Look out for a term called 'wagering requirement'. That stipulates how much you need to bet your original deposit and the free bets that you receive. The ideal scenario is that a bookmaker will allow you to keep any winnings that are made from a bonus bet. However, it's important to look for minimum odds that might be stipulated with either a qualifying wager or a free bet.

🔗📁He was aboard 2000 hero Papillon, trained by his father Ted Walsh and five years later, was successful on the Willie Mullins-trained Hedgehunter. 🔗📁The start will now be a standing start at the tape, rather than the traditional rolling start. This change is also designed to reduce the speed that horses arrive at the first obstacle. Each horse must have an official rating of at least 130 - rather than 125. Fence 11 has been reduced in height by two inches and will have the drop on the landing side reduced. Horses will no longer be led onto the course by a handler before the race, instead being released to canter in front of the grandstands. The start time has been moved from 5.15pm to 4pm.

🔗📁Honourable mention: Shakalakaboomboom The actual mathematical method Last year, Cambridge mathematician William Hartson attempted to create a formula that would predict the winner of the National. He reviewed the results of every race since 1886 and scored factors including bookies’ odds, how old the horse is, the letters in the owner’s name and the letters and number of words in the horses’ names to devise his formula. Cut a long story short, he predicted Seabass would win. Which, erm, he didn’t. However, this year, an updated formula for 2014 has put more emphasis on recent results and, critically, also takes into account horse trainers’ names. Which means it’s virtually foolproof. His predicted 2014 winner? Monberg Dude – part owned by Mike Tindall and ‘coached’ by Zara Phillips.

Both Protektorat and Le Milos provided first successes in those prestigious contests and Ashtown Lad gave Skelton a first success over the big Aintree obstacles. ‌ Despite reservations over his stamina – he had faded to be fifth in the Coral Scottish Grand National at Ayr in April – Ashtown Lad, who is owned by Aintree lover Darren Yates, is likely to be aimed at the world’s greatest steeplechase back in Liverpool on April 15 in the New Year. He could be real contender for the big one if he stays the extra distance having taken to the unique challenge so well. He was cut to 33-1 by Paddy Power for the National behind last year's winner Noble Yeats, who is as low as 8-1 following his earlier impressive victory in the Many Clouds Chase on his return to Aintree.

Racing in Ireland attempted to take place behind closed doors starting on March 29 - but that decision was changed after government cancelled all sporting events. The Dubai World Cup meeting will go ahead on March 28 'without paid hospitality spectators'.

🔗📁How long has Clare Balding been a journalist? An award-winning broadcaster, journalist and author, Clare Balding, 50, has been a fixture on television for decades. From 1988 until 1993, she was a leading amateur flat jockey and won an award for her memoir covering her time growing up in a racing yard. After studying at Cambridge University, Clare started working for the BBC as a trainee back in 1994. Clare is closely associated with horse racing (Picture: Getty Images) There she worked on 5 Live, Radio 1, Radio 2 and Radio 4. She made her television debut in 1995 – when she introduced highlights of Royal Ascot and has since been associated with coverage of horse racing events, like the Grand National.

🔗📁Racing will shake up its TV tender process this summer by asking broadcasters which races they want to bid for rather than restricting them to specific packages. The sport is not in a position to dictate terms, in contrast to football’s Premier League. The new going rate of £11million per live PL match dwarves the £4.8m per year C4 pay for their monopoly terrestrial coverage. And even such an outstanding day of racing as the opening Tuesday of the Cheltenham Festival saw a worrying drop in C4 viewing figures, with the peak of 910,000 a significant 71,000 down on the previous year’s figure.

🔗📁The teenage son of Grand National-winning trainer Henry de Bromhead died in a racing accident in Ireland on Saturday. Jack de Bromhead suffered fatal injuries after being thrown from his horse at the Glenbeigh Racing Festival in County Kerry. The racing festival programme was abandoned immediately while fellow trainer Gordon Elliott cancelled Sunday's open day at his yard as a mark of respect. Emergency services had been called to Rossbeigh beach — where the racing takes place — in Kerry after the incident on Saturday, when De Bromhead’s mount stumbled and ditched the youngster onto the sands. A spokesman for the festival committee told the Irish Mail on Sunday: ‘Many of the members of the Glenbeigh Race Committee are parents themselves and they are devastated at the tragic events.

🔗📁Thousands flocked to Aintree Racecourse for Grand National Day on Saturday with photos showing just how excited racegoers were about the big day. The sun came out for in the third day of the event for racegoers as they celebrated one of the most famous sporting events in the world. This year Corach Rambler won the renowned steeplechase race, with Vanillier in second and Big Dog third. Liverpool is no stranger to high profile names, but the festival seems to attract more than ever. A number of celebrities were spotted today, including actor Dominic West, Jorgie Porter, Christopher Biggins, Former football manager Steve Bruce, Harry Redknapp, Georgia 'Toff' Toffolo and more.

🔗📁Racegoer Clive Francis, 66 - who has been to every Grand National meeting in the last 40 years - said: “I swear it wasn’t like this last year. “We had to climb out of the car and switch the engine off while they searched inside and outside.” He joked: “One guard got panicky when he found a gun in my footwell - but calmed down when he saw it was a plastic water pistol my grandson got free with a comic! “Then after we parked up we had to have body searches. “They then checked my hold-all and finally swept me up and down with a metal detector. “I don’t think anyone will complain though as after the Brussels attacks we all want to feel safe.” Read more: Ladies flash their knickers and cleavage at Aintree first day Aintree officials said they were working “in tandem” with Merseyside Police and said “racegoers’ safety is paramount.” A Merseyside Police spokesman said: “The Grand National is one of the biggest events in the sporting calendar and consistently attracts more than 150,000 people during the three-day festival.

🔗📁Trainer Lucinda Russell is eyeing more glory over the Randox Grand National fences with Mighty Thunder in next month's Becher Chase at Aintree Racecourse. The Scottish-based trainer won the world's greatest steeplechase with One For Arthur at Aintree in 2017. And now she will send last season's Scottish Grand National hero for a first crack at the famous fences for the Becher Chase a week on Saturday. Having won at Ayr in the spring, the eight-year-old made his seasonal return when fourth to Fusil Raffles in the Grade Two Charlie Hall Chase at Wetherby at the end of last month.

🔗📁‌ Next up as Gosforth Park is the always-popular meeting to mark St Patrick’s Day. Taking place on Saturday, Pot of Gold’s racing entertainment will come with lots of Irish jigs and Guinness. 🔗📁The sheer quantity of mayhem in Friday’s Topham Chase was a useful and timely corrective for those tempted to present their Grand National conclusions with too much in the way of confidence. But if there is a horse in today’s field that I trust to navigate his way among the icebergs, it is The Druids Nephew (4.15). He was last seen taking on 23 rivals at the Cheltenham Festival, looking at ease and in control throughout.

🔗📁‌ ‌ View 4 Images Major changes have been made to the Grand National (Image: Getty Images) What are the changes to the 2024 Grand National? Significant changes have been made. The alterations have been made after animal rights protesters ambushed the event last year - causing a delay of over 15 minutes. ‌ However, the Jockey Club insists that the changes did not come as a direct response to those protests. The most significant changes are as follows: The field has been reduced from 40 horses to a maximum of 34. The first fence has been brought forward, towards the start line, by 60 yards in order to reduce the speed at which the horses reach it.

The Cheltenham Festival went ahead amid some criticism before the social distancing measures were tightened. The Japan Racing Association revealed that 'government-sanctioned races' will go ahead behind closed doors. Racing in Ireland attempted to take place behind closed doors starting on March 29 - but that decision was changed after government cancelled all sporting events. The Dubai World Cup meeting will go ahead on March 28 'without paid hospitality spectators'.

🔗📁Fourth horse dies after Grand National Two horses have died following the main event after two fatalities earlier in the festival A fourth horse has died after failing to recover from injuries sustained at the Grand National. Eclair Surf suffered a heavy fall at the third fence in Saturday’s race. ‌ His trainer Emma Lavelle announced the news on Twitter on Sunday morning. “We are very sad to report that having sustained a traumatic head injury in yesterday's Grand National, Eclair Surf lost his fight this morning. ‌ “He was looked after at the racecourse by a team of first-class vets before being transferred to Liverpool University who treated him all night, however very sadly it was not to be. He was an incredibly special horse, loved by everyone and he will be missed terribly.”

🔗📁19:15 Lottie Gibbons 90 pictures of racegoers having the time of their lives at Aintree The Grand National Festival has wrapped up for another year. The racing event attracted 150,000 to Aintree and, as ever, it was memorable. The world's greatest steeplechase saw an incredible achievement from trainer Willie Mullins who had four of the first five finishers. Nick Rockett led home an extraordinary one-two-three for Mullins at 33-1, ridden by the his son, Patrick Mullins. Racegoers roared home the horses as they raced towards the finishing line. It has been an action-packed Grand National Festival and racegoers have been pictured each day having the time of their lives.

🔗📁To no one’s great surprise, the card at Catterick has failed to pass an inspection and the turf cards scheduled for Musselburgh and Market Rasen on Wednesday have also been abandoned. Chelmsford City, however, will race on the all-weather as planned, which means that with Lingfield also getting the go-ahead, racing will defy the Beast with a total of 13 races on Tuesday. Jorvik Dancer (4.15) is probably the pick of the prices in the sprint handicap at Chelmsford City. He completed a swift hat-trick in late December and early January but remains fairly weighted on the pick of his recent form and is a fair bet at around 11-4. Carolinae (3.30) should also go well at Lingfield, but with the Cheltenham Festival now imminent, punters may well spend some time instead looking at the ante-post markets. Willie Mullins, the leading trainer at the Festival in four of the last five seasons, opened his doors to the media on Monday, and here is a round-up of his comments on some of his leading contenders.

🔗📁Geraghty, in fact, was more dependable than Walsh when he got on a Cheltenham Festival favourite, with a 48% strike-rate on clear favourites from 2003 onwards. Walsh’s strike-rate on clear favourites over the same period was 41%. But while Geraghty rode 39 market leaders in that time, Walsh was aboard 86. Geraghty had not been riding since jump racing resumed in Ireland last month and while the last mount of his exceptional career was pulled up at Uttoxeter on 14 March, his final ride at the Cheltenham Festival a day earlier was a winner (and favourite): Saint Roi, who landed a big gamble in the McManus colours in the County Hurdle.

🔗📁Newsboy's ITV4 tips for Tuesday, including Welsh Grand National selection from Chepstow The Big Dog carries Newsboy's hopes in the Welsh Grand National at Chepstow, plus tips from Tuesday's other meetings THE BIG DOG can give his rivals weight and a beating in the Coral Welsh Grand National Handicap Chase (2.50) at Chepstow today. Trained in Co Kildare by Peter Fahey, the nine-year-old followed a head margin in the Munster National at Limerick in October with a three-and-a-half-length call in Navan’s Troytown Handicap Chase at the end of last month. Top weight and a 5lb higher mark may not be enough to stop Aidan Coleman’s mount from racking up the hat-trick. The Grade 2 Coral Finale Junior Hurdle (1.40) ranks as a good opportunity for COMFORT ZONE to resume winning ways after a last-time-out third to subsequent Grade 1 scorer Lossiemouth at Fairyhouse. The returning RED ROOKIE looks well treated in the Coral Get Closer To The Action Handicap Chase (1.05), and JUST A DIME is taken to prove ahead of the assessor in the Coral Racing Club Handicap Hurdle (2.10).

🔗📁The white box tells everyone arriving at the enclosure that Ascot Racecourse is a drug free zone and that illicit substances can be dropped through the slot in the top of the white box. But the box itself is only locked by a cable tie. Yesterday was Gold Cup Day, commonly known as Ladies’ Day, but there was little evidence of ladylike – or gentlemanly – behaviour as the event ended in two arrests. In a blatant disregard for Ascot’s strict behavioural code, a drunken brawl broke out by a Victorian band stand. Eight men started to fight on the lawn by a champagne bar just yards from the The Royal Mile, Ascot’s home straight. Terrified racegoers fled to avoid being struck by stray punches as the drunken group, some egged on by female friends, armed themselves with bottles and chair legs.

🔗📁And that was proved as under Harry Cobden he came home by a comfortable six lengths from Ree Oka (6-1) with Doctor Ken (3-1) a neck back in third. Trainer Nicholls was at his 'home' track of Wincanton near his Ditcheat stables so his assistant Harry Derham was on hand to witness Gellino Bello's fine debut over hurdles. He said: "It was a nice performance. His bumper was good for a horse who we never thought would never be much of a bumper horse really. ‌ He jumped beautifully. Harry (Cobden) got him in a nice position and he is a very, very relaxed horse. It is a big long galloping straight where you are going to have to stay well. And he does stay well. He probably showed a turn of foot we probably thought might not be there. So he is an exciting horse."

🔗📁When the Americans announced the ‘strategic review’ last year they may well have expected a Grand National. In an indication of how there was only one show in town, not long after the announcement rivals Liverpool were taken off the market. But what they got has turned out to be a two-horse race. There is no tech giant. No Apple, no Amazon. While there are minor differences, the final bids from Qatar’s Sheikh and Britain’s Sir Jim Ratcliffe value the club at around £5bn. This is not what the Glazers were seeking. Insiders believe that figure was closer to £6bn.
